newsitem.title: UK: Capacity shortage boosts UK-LatAm air cargo rates.
newsitem.headline: Capacity shortage boosts UK-LatAm air cargo rates.

text.p: Lack of capacity has been a key factor in lifting air cargo rates from the UK to Latin America, a Reuters survey shows.

But ex-UK rates to the United States, with the exception of the west coast, and also to Johannesburg and Nairobi, have been on the decline due to excess capacity and resultant stiff competition amongst carriers.

"Air cargo is a feast and famine business, dependent on available capacity. (For South America) the keyword now is 'famine'," Gerry Burgin, managing director of leading forwarder Wilson & Co (UK), told Reuters.

Air cargo growth from Britain to Latin America is restricted as capacity is mainly limited to the bellyholds of passenger aircraft, which have high passenger and baggage loads at a time of year when frequencies are often reduced.

"It is certainly difficult to obtain space at the moment from the UK to Buenos Aires," said a cargo spokesman for Spain's Iberia, owner of a 10 percent stake in Argentine airline Aerolineas Argentinas, for which it acts as UK agent.

Iberia's UK-Argentina cargo either flies from London to Madrid on Iberia flights for transfer on to daily onward Aerolineas Boeing 747-200 passenger services to Buenos Aires, or goes on three-times-weekly London-Madrid-Buenos Aires 747-200 services operated by Aerolineas.
"Either way, it is a problem obtaining space, especially on the Aerolineas flights from London, which can't take much cargo," the spokesman added.

Despite pricing competition coming from continental European carriers serving Argentina, the general overall lack of capacity has seen the average per kg rate for a 100 kg shipment on the route rise two pence to 2.21 stg since last month.
Observers say there is more competition available from the UK to Brazil, a much larger air cargo market than Argentina, with many transhipment services being provided via Europe and/or Miami.

But this does not mean there is an over-abundance of capacity and, with per kg prices ranging from 2.00 to 2.50 stg a kilo depending on the routing and service quality, the average rate to Sao Paulo has held at 2.10 stg.
And it is likely to continue to be firm, especially as British Airways has decided to increase its UK-South America cargo rates by 10 percent from March 17.
Varig Brazilian Airlines said it had no plans to raise its ex-UK cargo rates, which it said had been higher than BA's to Brazil for a number of years.

"We are getting reasonable yields on the route, the market is strong -- especially for automotive parts made in the UK for assembly in Brazil -- and it is still growing," Varig's UK cargo manager Paul Ryan said.
After the usual slow January period, "February was extremely good and we are very optimistic for the rest of the year," he said.
Cargolux is also benefiting from the Europe-Brazil auto parts boom, its UK cargo services spokesman Daren Kilgour said.

"We only started operating three-times-a-week from Luxembourg to Sao Paulo five months ago and, from the UK, we are already sending 10 to 25 tonnes a week on these flights," he said, adding that the carrier's recently started weekly Luxembourg-Santiago service had helped open up a small but expanding market for the UK operation.
Richard Wright, of Globe Air Cargo, UK GSA for Tampa Airlines of Florida said sterling's strength was not having an impact on the Latam market.

"Tampa's key market is Colombia, followed by Peru and Ecuador, and we use several airlines to ship freight from the UK to connect with its ex-Miami DC-8F and Boeing 707 freighter flights," said Wright.
"We've been quite busy of late. December was a good month and January/February was strong, although this has traditionally been a slow period for the air cargo industry," he noted.
BA World Cargo managing director Kevin Hatton told Reuters recently that for his division, Latin America had had "a great year", with both Chile and Colombia standing out.
Continental Airlines' UK cargo manager Brian Coleman said that for him, Latin America is a small market due to capacity restrictions.
From Britain, Continental's DC-10's are linked to Latin America via Newark and Houston by limited capacity Boeing 757 and 737 passenger connections.

Coleman said he was "very interested" in developing this business and hoped that, before too long, the airline would start flights across the Atlantic and then down to Latin America using wide-body 777s offering generous cargo space.

Continental's UK-New York (Newark) cargo business is "doing reasonably well". On its U.S. routes, Continental is offering 20 percent reductions on Mondays and Tuesdays and 10 percent off on Wednesdays and Thursdays, with the full tariff being adhered to Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays.
"I don't think this is the result of BA's discounting scheme that is currently underway. It is just that at this time of the year, customers expect spot (cut) prices," he said.

"And we are flexible on certain days when we have the capacity available. From London Gatwick and Manchester, we are this year operating 134 flights to Newark and Houston, up 54 percent on 1996, and this represents an 87 percent rise in cargo capacity," said Coleman.
The average London-New York per kg rate for a 100 kg shipment has slipped two pence over the past fortnight to 0.63 stg.
For 1,000 kg plus, the per kg industry-wide average is 0.48 stg, with regular contract customers getting around 0.45 stg per kg.
El Al Israel Airlines' UK cargo manager Jacob Pianko said business to New York is weaker now than two to three months ago.
"For us, this market is not so strong at present," he said, adding that both strong competition and the high value of sterling were the reasons.
He said that because of the strength of the pound, he had noticed that many U.S. importers had booked cargo capacity from continental Europe rather than the UK.

Cargolux's Kilgour said that the extent of competition between Europe and New York had restricted his carrier to operating just one weekly Boeing 747-400 Luxembourg-JFK (via Reykjavik) freighter service.
From the UK, he added, the input for this flight was relatively minor, comprising mainly "offside cargo" -- shipments too large to fit into the bellyholds of passenger planes.
But to the U.S. west coast, Kilgour said Cargolux was experiencing good ex-UK loads and yields.
"We operate two weekly 747-400 freighter services from Prestwick to Seattle carrying an increasing amount of cargo for Boeing -- smokescreens, aircraft engines, toilet units and so on," he said.

The carrier also operates two direct weekly Luxembourg-Los Angeles 747F flights and Kilgour said that from the UK, the carrier was benefiting from an increasing number of horse shipments booked on behalf of the LA Jockey Club.

"After just 'dribs-and-drabs' business from the UK, these horse shipments have really grown in importance over the past 18 months and they are now regular consignments, as are aircraft spares and parts shipments," he said.
"Recently, we have regularly been shipping two to three 'stables' (three horses in each) a week from the Britain, building up to the two-year-old horse sales in LA in March," he added.

El Al's Pianko said the strength of sterling was having the same adverse effect on his business to the U.S. west coast, trucked from the UK to Frankfurt and Amsterdam to connect with weekly 747-200F services from each city to Los Angeles, as it was to New York.
"It is cheaper for U.S. companies to buy in Germany and the Netherlands than it is here," he said.
BA's Hatton has said that his carrier's cargo business to the U.S. west coast had been weak over the past year, while the central region was a strong market.

Continental has seen reasonably healthy air cargo trading from the UK to Chicago, to where it trucks cargo from New York, despite strong competition from the likes of United, American Airlines and BA (all direct), Air Canada (trucked via Toronto) and TWA (trucked via Minneapolis).
The extent of this competition has pushed the average per kg rate for a 100 kg shipment down two pence since February 13 to 0.74 stg.
Continental's Coleman said he was also experiencing a growth in hi-tech shipments from the UK to Cleveland, Milwaukee and Indianapolis.
Ever since South African air transport deregulation in 1995, ever-increasing competition has been forcing air cargo rates -- and passenger fares -- down, say observers.
"And that isn't the only factor behind this trend," said Len Bunn of Air Marketing Associates, UK cargo agent for Air Namibia, which serves Johannesburg from the UK via Windhoek.
"The exchange rate of the rand against sterling is awful," he said, adding that this had badly affected UK-South Africa air cargo business.
He said that Air Namibia was "holding its own" during these difficult times on the route, although "yields are down".

The state of the UK-South Africa air cargo market shows no signs of improving, say market sources, especially as Virgin Atlantic has just increased to six its former three-times-weekly London-Johannesburg Airbus A340 services and will boost the frequency to daily from July 15.
Extremely competitive ex-UK rates to South Africa are currently being offered by carriers as diverse as Saudi Arabian Airlines, which tranships via Jeddah, and Alitalia via Rome.
"This market is very saturated," said Gil Harding, of Air Gabon's UK cargo GSA, ANA Marketing Services.
"Consequently, Air Gabon will be holding its present cargo rates on the route until July, a year after starting up these flights from the UK," he added.
Meanwhile, from London to Nairobi, Harding - also DAS Air Cargo's management agent - said this market remained unstable as national political elections results are still awaited.

The average per kg rate per 100 kg on this route has fallen two pence to 0.93 stg since earlier this month, due both to the aforementioned marketplace instability coupled with rising rate competition.
On the UK-Sweden air cargo market, the average rate has dipped two pence to 0.73 stg, mainly due to the off-peak season and competition between Air France, Lufthansa, British Airways and Finnair.
But it has firmed at 0.70 to Copenhagen.
Overall Brad Brennan, sales and marketing manager in the UK of Swedish forwarder ASG said the state of the market in general, was "healthy".
"But it is becoming more and more difficult for ex-UK airfreight services to compete with (forwarder/trucking) companies like Danzas and Europa from the UK to Denmark," he said.
